# Pause Before Consensus: Testing Batch-Released Deliberation in Journal Peer Review

## Summary

Peer-review reform usually focuses on who reviewers are, whether their names are disclosed, or how editors select them. This project instead examines the timing of reviewer interaction. In many editorial systems, the first reviewer to enter a discussion can frame the manuscript’s central problem before other reviewers have stated their positions. Later comments may then converge on that framing, even when initial reports emphasized different issues.

The proposed study will test a “batch-release” discussion protocol. Reviewers will submit short opening positions that remain sealed until every participating reviewer has responded or a 36-hour window expires. The statements will then be displayed simultaneously in randomized order. This protocol will be compared with an otherwise similar discussion in which each opening statement appears as soon as it is submitted. The study asks whether removing a temporally privileged first voice preserves independent information, changes editorial decisions, and improves agreement with a later assessment panel.

## Rationale

Reviewer disagreement is commonly treated as a problem to be resolved. Yet some disagreement reflects complementary expertise rather than error. A methods reviewer may identify an estimation problem while a domain reviewer notices that the research question is unimportant. If the first discussion comment defines one concern as decisive, other concerns may receive less attention without being answered.

Research on group judgment suggests that early statements can anchor later discussion, but journal peer review is an unusual setting: participants have already produced independent reports, possess unequal expertise, and know that an editor rather than the group makes the final decision. Findings from ordinary committees therefore may not transfer directly. A change to discussion timing is also comparatively inexpensive. It does not require publishing reviewer identities, recruiting additional reviewers, or changing a journal’s acceptance threshold.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The study will address three questions:

1. Does batch release reduce the influence of the earliest commenter on reviewers’ final recommendations?
2. Does it preserve a wider range of substantively distinct concerns without reducing useful consensus?
3. Do decisions reached under batch release correspond more closely to an independent panel’s later assessment?

The main hypothesis is that final recommendations in the conventional condition will be disproportionately associated with the earliest commenter’s pre-discussion score. Batch release is expected to weaken this association. It is also expected to increase the number of distinct concerns carried into the editor’s decision letter, while adding no more than one day to median decision time.

## Study design

The Meridian Editorial Cooperative, an invented consortium of twelve mid-volume journals in environmental engineering, computational linguistics, and behavioral economics, will participate for eighteen months. The target sample is 1,200 manuscripts that reach discussion with at least three completed reviews. Desk rejections, single-reviewer decisions, and manuscripts requiring an immediate ethics referral will be excluded.

Manuscripts will be randomized within journal and calendar month after all initial reports have been filed. In both conditions, reviewers will receive the same prompt asking for a 150-word opening position containing: a provisional recommendation on a five-point scale, the most decision-relevant concern, and one reason their recommendation might change.

In the sequential condition, each opening position will become visible to the other reviewers when submitted. In the batch-release condition, positions will remain sealed until all reviewers respond or 36 hours pass. Released statements will appear together in a computer-randomized order. Editors will be asked not to intervene before the opening stage closes. Afterward, both groups will use the journal’s ordinary unstructured discussion interface for up to five days. Editors will retain full authority over decisions.

Reviewers will be informed about the study when accepting the assignment and may decline participation without declining the review. Editors cannot be blinded because the interface will display the assigned protocol. Authors will not be told the condition until the study concludes, and the condition will not affect what information appears in decision letters.

## Measures

The primary behavioral outcome will be “first-position pull”: the extent to which reviewers’ final scores move toward the pre-discussion score of the earliest commenter in the sequential condition, compared with movement toward a randomly designated position in the batch-release condition. The model will adjust for every reviewer’s initial score, self-rated expertise, report length, and the initial distance between reviewers.

Secondary outcomes will include change in score dispersion, discussion length, time to decision, reviewer satisfaction, and the number of distinct concerns appearing both in discussion and in the editor’s letter. Two trained coders, unaware of condition, will classify concerns into design, analysis, interpretation, novelty, presentation, and ethics categories. Twenty percent of discussions will be double-coded, with disagreements resolved by a third coder. An exploratory text-similarity analysis will estimate whether later comments reuse the first commenter’s framing.

Decision quality will be estimated for a stratified random subset of 180 manuscripts. Six months after the original decision, a three-person assessment panel will receive the anonymized initial manuscript, revision if one exists, and editor letter, but not the original reviewer discussion or experimental condition. The panel will rate methodological soundness, contribution, and whether the original editorial decision was defensible. Distance between the editor’s decision and the panel median will serve as the principal quality measure. For accepted papers, eighteen-month citation counts and formal corrections will be recorded as exploratory outcomes.

## Analysis and sample size

The primary analysis will follow assignment regardless of whether all reviewers submit an opening position. A multilevel regression will include random intercepts for journal, editor, reviewer, and manuscript, since some reviewers and editors will appear repeatedly. Interaction terms will examine whether effects differ by initial disagreement, reviewer expertise, and field. The coding and analysis plan will be registered before outcomes are inspected.

With 1,200 manuscripts and an anticipated 15% rate of incomplete opening statements, the study is expected to have 80% power to detect a difference of approximately 0.14 standard deviations in first-position pull. This calculation treats manuscripts as independent and will be revised after the cooperative supplies estimates of repeat-reviewer frequency. No adjustment is planned for the exploratory subgroup comparisons.

## Practical and ethical considerations

Batch release may delay discussion when one reviewer does not respond. The 36-hour release rule limits this cost, and automatic reminders will be sent after 24 hours. A technical log will record accidental early disclosure, editor intervention, and interface failures. Manuscripts affected by such failures will remain in the main analysis but will also be examined separately.

The principal ethical concern is that authors are exposed to an unproven process. Both protocols preserve ordinary editorial authority, and editors may end discussion immediately if delay would harm an author. Reviewer comments and identifiers will be stored separately, and published results will aggregate journals unless a journal requests attribution.

## Limitations

The intervention combines two features—simultaneous release and randomized display order—so the study may not identify which feature causes any observed effect. The assessment panel is also another form of peer review rather than an objective measure of correctness. Because only twelve volunteer journals participate, results may not generalize to high-volume, highly selective, or non-English-language venues. Reviewers who consent to the experiment may be unusually comfortable with structured deliberation, and awareness of observation could make both conditions more careful than normal.

## Outputs

The project will produce a reusable discussion module, an anonymized dataset of score changes and coded concerns, and a protocol that journals can adapt without altering anonymity policies. If batch release reduces first-position pull without delaying decisions or lowering panel agreement, the cooperative will test it as the default discussion setting for a further year.
planted_strengths: Chooses a specific and relatively neglected mechanism in peer-review reform: the temporal ordering of deliberation rather than anonymity or reviewer selection.
Uses manuscript-level randomization, stratification by journal and month, a common prompt across conditions, and an intention-to-treat analysis.
Collects multiple kinds of outcomes, including score movement, decision time, coded substantive concerns, reviewer experience, and a blinded later assessment.
Anticipates implementation issues such as nonresponse, accidental disclosure, editor intervention, repeated reviewers, and discussion delays.
Includes transparent limitations, preregistration, coding reliability procedures, and a plausible low-cost path to adoption.
planted_weaknesses: The intervention bundles simultaneous release with randomized display order, preventing clean identification of the mechanism while the hypotheses emphasize timing specifically.

The proposed assessment panel is essentially another peer-review process and is a circular, weak proxy for true decision quality; it also sees revisions and editor letters that may bias retrospective judgment.
The power calculation initially treats manuscripts as independent despite repeated reviewers, editors, and journal-level clustering, and it is not based on a clearly justified effect-size estimate.

The first-position-pull measure is complicated and not fully comparable across arms because the treatment condition has a randomly designated or displayed position rather than a genuine first speaker.

quality_rationale: The proposal has a worthwhile, non-obvious reform target and a reasonably concrete randomized field design. Its standardized prompts, operational safeguards, multilevel analysis plan, blinded coding, and explicit limitations provide genuine methodological value. However, its central causal contrast bundles two interface changes, its primary anchoring metric is awkward across conditions, and its purported decision-quality benchmark remains another subjective review. The rough power calculation does not yet account properly for clustering, while volunteer participation, unblinded editors, and a short citation window further weaken inference. These merits and shortcomings support a mid-range score.
